name: Unfollowing comparison accounts

lead: This means unfollowing or muting accounts that make you compare your looks unfavourably. The payoff people want is a calmer self-image and less body dissatisfaction day to day.

The chain is removing comparison-triggering accounts, less exposure to idealised images, then a better body and face image. A systematic review of 43 experimental studies, summarised on Wikipedia, links viewing idealised images on social networking sites with higher body dissatisfaction in young adults, with appearance comparison identified as an important factor. Unfollowing itself has not been tested as an intervention.

paras: People go through their following list and unfollow or mute accounts that leave them feeling worse about their appearance, and sometimes follow accounts on other topics instead. Some do this alongside a time limit on apps or a short break.
No physical risks. Long-term effects of content exposure remain unclear, and findings on body-positive content are mixed.

angle.text: People prune their feeds of accounts that provoke appearance comparison to get a healthier view of their own face and body. Experiments link idealised imagery to body dissatisfaction; unfollowing itself has not been studied.

lead: Unfollowing comparison accounts is the practice of removing or muting social media accounts, such as influencers, models and fitness creators, whose posts make someone feel their own face or body falls short. People do it to protect how they see their own appearance and to keep motivation focused on their own progress, so that time spent on self-improvement is not undermined by constant comparison.

A 2025 meta-analysis of 20 experiments with 3,603 young women, as summarised on Wikipedia, found that exposure to idealised body content on social media lowered body satisfaction [1]. An earlier systematic review of 43 experiments (8,637 participants) linked idealised images on social networking sites to higher body dissatisfaction in young adults and identified appearance comparison as the key mechanism [1]. Wikipedia also reports that photo-based apps such as Instagram and Snapchat were found to affect men's body image more negatively than non-photo apps [1].
No study found tests unfollowing itself. A T Nation article discusses a study on whether fitness selfies motivate or de-motivate viewers [2].
infobox: Experiments on idealised images and body satisfaction [1]

paras: The practice includes unfollowing, muting, or replacing accounts that produce comparison, and following accounts with more varied appearances. A 2021 scoping review cited on Wikipedia found images without people, and images showing non-conventional appearances, were the most promising for body image, while evidence on captions and hashtags was limited or inconsistent [1]. A 2025 meta-analysis found body-positive content produced a modest improvement, weaker on TikTok than on Instagram [1].

Reviews link viewing idealised images with higher body dissatisfaction, with appearance comparison as an important factor, and report mixed findings on body-positive content and unclear long-term effects [1]. For men, studies describe a desire for more muscle, with peers having strong influence on body criticism and following celebrities affecting male body image [1]. Ferguson, Winegard and Winegard (2011) argue that peer effects matter more than media effects and that media influence is overstated; more than 40 measurement instruments are in use [1].
No studies found on unfollowing as an intervention. Related experiments on exposure to idealised images and body satisfaction are summarised in reference works [1].
